A stimulus is an object, event or situation which causes a person or an animal to behave in a particular way.

�

A stimulus could be

  • a red light,�
  • a ringing telephone,�
  • a waving hand.

A response is the way a person or animal behaves towards, or as a result of, the stimulus.�

Such as:

  • moving your foot from the gas pedal to the brake pedal,�
  • running around the house looking for the telephone,
  • waving back.�

If a situation (stimulus) occurs and a young child responds to it in a favourable way, a parent might attempt to strengthen that connection by providing reinforcement.

Reinforcement is a process that increases the chances of a certain behavior occurring again.

For example, there is a pile of toys in the living room (stimulus), the child puts them away in the toy box (response). The parent is pleased with the child s behavior and rewards the child with a cookie and praise (reinforcement).

Types of Reinforcement

Remember, reinforcement increases a response. This is true of both positive AND negative reinforcement.�

  • A cookie, a hug, getting extra privileges at home, and an allowance are all example of positive reinforcement�(something is added to increase the behaviour).�
  • A negative reinforcement includes anything negative that is removed from the environment like loud noises, physical pain, punishment, or annoyances of any kind (something is subtracted to increase the behaviour).�

Since negative reinforcement is a little more difficult to visualize, here are some examples:

  • A little girl knows that if she picks up all of her toys she won t get a scolding. Removing the threat of a scolding encourages her to behave in a favourable way.
  • You fell and broke your arm while skating.�The pain is intense and you think the pain of having the bone set will be even worse.�You go to the doctor anyway, believing that enduring more pain will help ease your pain long-term.
